paragraphs: By the end of summer in the second year of Long’an, the Huai River had fallen far enough to bare a sandy ridge in midstream. Reed roots whitened across the shallows. Fish stranded in muddy hollows turned their silver bellies toward the sky. Boatmen, feeling the hard knock of their bamboo poles against the bottom, scarcely recognized the waterway. In past years they could have sailed it through layers of mist without losing their bearings. Now the channels had shifted, and a boat crossing an old shoal could ground with a moment’s inattention.
Outside the city of Xuyi, people had greater trouble finding water than the fish.

More than a hundred families had spent two nights beneath the city gate with quilts, basins, jars, and torn mats. Some carried children; one man pulled the carcass of his plow ox, hoping to exchange its hide for grain. But the shops within the walls had all lowered their shutters. Soldiers looked down upon the crowd. Those who had eaten breakfast before taking their morning watch still urged them to go home; the men replacing them in the afternoon would hardly speak.
Xu Sanniang came up holding her youngest son and called toward the wall, “Xu Cheng is an archer in the Left Camp. Call him for me.”

A soldier on the wall recognized the name. When Xu Cheng received his pay, he always set a little aside to send to his wife and children. But the commandant stood nearby, and the soldier dared only shake his head. “No one is allowed out of camp.”
“I’m not asking him to come out. My boy is burning with fever. Tell him to beg the army doctor for a little medicine.”
“The army doctor has no medicine left either,” the soldier whispered.
Whether Xu Sanniang heard him was impossible to tell. She stayed at the foot of the wall, the child’s face pressed against her shoulder, his heat so fierce that it numbed the skin over her breast.

In his office, Lu Yan, prefect of Xuyi, opened an edict from Jiankang. It had passed through three relay stations, all the clay seals intact; the imperial stamp at the end blazed red. Every border city was to hold its frontier. Civilian boats were forbidden to cross without permission. Anyone dealing privately with Qin territory was to be investigated for collusion with the enemy.

The assistant prefect asked what should be done about the people outside. Lu Yan first asked how much grain remained. The granary officer counted seventeen thousand hu. Once rations for the garrison, fodder for the animals, and the costs of defending the walls were deducted, there was enough for three thousand troops for only two months. If another border alarm came before winter, it might not last one.
“And this summer’s harvest?”
“Three tenths of what we usually collect. The requisition for army grain remains at the old amount.”

Lu Yan fell silent. He knew perfectly well that people were hungry. Last year the Huai had burst its embankments; the ridges in the fields had not yet been restored, and now drought had come. The granaries behind the high walls of wealthy households were guarded by private retainers. When officials called, the great families produced only last year’s moldy grain. In poorer kitchens there remained little besides grass and bran, yet county collectors still demanded millet.
“Keep the gates closed,” Lu Yan said. “Take every ferry into the government landing. Limit sales from the shops; reduce army rations. Send those outside back to their villages.”
“There is no food in their villages,” the assistant prefect said.

“Will standing under the walls produce any?” Lu Yan tapped the granary figures. “Let them in today, and tomorrow the wives and children of our soldiers must share their grain. If Qin horsemen cross in the confusion, the court’s first question will be who lost Xuyi.”

There was no easy answer to that. Still the assistant prefect did not withdraw. His own mother had died in a village outside the town the year before. Labor levies had been so confused at the time of her burial that he could not even find an intact coffin. Many faces at the gate looked like those of her neighbors.
“Could we at least admit the families of military households to seek treatment?”
Lu Yan studied him. “Draft a procedure. It must not disrupt the garrison.”

Before he could draft one, another order arrived from Jiankang demanding a count of fugitive households. Lu Yan called him back. They calculated through the night, but he could not bring himself to put his name to the order that would admit the people.
More than a hundred li away, the gates of Shanyang stood open.

County magistrate Du Qian was standing before the granary himself, rice bran clinging to his robe hem. Two small scales stood outside the doors; one clerk weighed grain while another entered names in the distribution register. The old and the young received food first, two sheng each per day. Able-bodied men were given less, and families with a sick member got another ladle of gruel. Stewards of several great households waited nearby, complaining that the magistrate would exhaust the county’s stores by feeding refugees. Du Qian told them to bring the harvest accounts from their villages: only after the numbers had been checked could they discuss whether a loan was justified. The men stalked off in anger.
A messenger from Jiankang rode through the crowd waiting for grain. Seeing that the official granary seals had been broken, his face hardened.
“You opened the military stores?”

Du Qian waited until the granary clerk had finished recording the day’s allotments before receiving the edict beneath the gallery. When the messenger had read it aloud, he ordered the stores sealed at once and all correspondence for buying grain from Qin halted. Du Qian knelt to acknowledge the command, then rose and asked, “The measure already on the scales today—may we finish distributing it?”
“You dare disobey an edict?”
“The grain has been assigned to people by name. They are waiting outside.”

The messenger accused him of buying loyalty with state grain. Once the stores were empty, he said, Qin troops would come upriver. Du Qian did not argue. He lifted the curtain and pointed to an ox cart newly brought beside the granary doors. Three villagers lay upon it. One girl was alive, clutching a half-filled jar of grass roots softened by rain. The other two lay under coarse linen, flies crawling on the shaft of the cart.

Du Qian ordered hot gruel for the girl first. The messenger looked at the granary, already one-third empty, and gripped the edict more tightly. In the end he did not stop them. The people in the queue never knew how close they had come to losing their rations. They worried only whether any rice would remain in the pot by the time their turn came.

Du Qian sent two county clerks north across the river. They carried no declaration of surrender, only quantities of grain and a price list for salt and cloth. Beneath it Du Qian had written that Shanyang could repay the debt over three years, that Qin grain might enter the county, and that Qin soldiers must not cross with the boats. Before the clerks left, he stamped the reverse with the county seal.
“Magistrate, are you pledging your official cap as security?” the registrar asked.
“I fear it is already pledged.” Du Qian put the seal back in its case. “What else do I have to pledge?”

When the Qin commandant on the north bank received the price list, his first impulse was to laugh. Shanyang had fewer than a thousand troops, empty granaries, and a starving population, yet its demands were firmer than those of most envoys. His deputy proposed sending five hundred horsemen to escort the grain across. With troops at its walls, Shanyang could be taken without loosing an arrow.
“Where is the grain to come from?” the commandant asked first.
“We still have some in the stores. The harvest was better north of the Huai.”
“And your troop-movement tally?”
The deputy laughed. “Five hundred men are hardly a campaign by the whole empire. In an emergency we can use our discretion.”

The commandant did not laugh. In his younger days he had fought under Murong Chui in the new army and had seen how a forged order changing the guard had opened half of Chang’an. He settled the visiting clerks in suitable quarters, sealed the price list, and sent it to Chang’an for verification along with the deputy’s proposal to advance on the city.

Ten days later the answer reached the ferry. One letter authorized thirty thousand hu of grain, valued against salt and cloth and handed over in installments. Southern boats would come to load it; Qin soldiers were not to cross the Huai. The other bore a short note in the Heavenly King’s own hand. After reading them, the commandant had a scribe copy the terms onto the ferry gate, lest someone later claim to have heard only half.

When the first grain sacks reached the river, the main body of Qin troops indeed remained three li away. Only granary clerks, boatmen, and measurers stood on the landing. Du Qian crossed to inspect the grain. He took a handful of sun-warmed millet from an open sack and held it in his palm. In a famine year, even clean grain felt like a precious luxury.
“And there is no condition requiring a garrison?” he asked.
“Chang’an’s instructions are plain,” the Qin commandant replied. “You repay the debt; the grain is yours. Whether anyone chooses to join Qin is a separate matter.”

A junior clerk traveling with Du Qian turned away to wipe his eyes. Du Qian offered no ceremonial thanks; he ordered the sacks loaded at once. It rained again the next day. A squall struck the boats midway across, and Du Qian himself caught a sack slipping over the gunwale, rubbing blisters raw on both hands.

Steam rose once more from Shanyang’s gruel stations. Some townspeople were grateful; others were furious. An elderly scholar with white hair leaned on his staff and cursed Du Qian for buying grain from Qin and betraying the legitimate dynasty. A woman beside him had just received three sheng of millet. “My son has eaten nothing for three days,” she said. “Let me cook his gruel today. If I have the strength tomorrow, sir, I will listen to your lecture.” She walked away, too exhausted even to quarrel.
News traveled more slowly than the grain boats to Xuyi, but in time it arrived.

Twenty-seven people had already starved outside the walls. At first someone still carried away the bodies; later they were covered with mats where they lay. Xu Sanniang’s youngest boy remained feverish. She soaked her last piece of cloth and laid it across his forehead; before the cloth cooled, it grew hot again. Looking through an opening in the battlements, Xu Cheng recognized his wife’s voice below. At night he lowered a small packet of spent medicinal herbs, for which his squad leader gave him twenty strokes of the military cudgel.

Lu Yan ordered a search for grain. In his register he called it a purchase against future compensation: each household would retain three days’ food, the government would buy the rest at a set price, and vouchers could be redeemed later. But by the time the order reached the market, soldiers were seizing grain faster than they could explain the word purchase. An old woman selling flatbread clutched a half-sack of wheat flour beneath her stove and was shoved to the ground. Her son raised a rolling pin to defend her and was cut down. Once blood appeared in the street, the alarm gong rang. More and more people gathered, cries to open the granary and open the city gates merging into one.

Lu Yan hurried to the market, intending to explain that the garrison stores could barely sustain the defense. But the hungry families of his own soldiers had already heard about Shanyang’s Qin grain. A voice called from the crowd, “They can eat gruel in Shanyang. Are we in Xuyi fit only to wait for death?”

Lu Yan ordered the speaker identified. As the soldiers pushed forward, a stone struck a commandant above the eyebrow. Swords came out; cries and fire rose together. Some ran toward the east gate, others dragged their children through the streets in search of relatives. The defenders formed a line in the gateway, but the sobbing of their own families soon broke it apart.

He Cheng, commandant at the east gate, drew his sword and shouted that anyone who approached the gate bar would be treated as a mutineer. He had fears of his own. Open the gate today, let refugees and rebellious soldiers pour out, and if Qin came tomorrow, his head alone would answer for the imperial command. He was not a cruel officer in ordinary times, but his wife and children lived in Jiankang. He neither knew nor wished to know whose mother any old woman outside might be.
A young soldier knelt before him. “Commandant, my mother is outside.”
“Back in line!”
“She was still calling my name last night.”

He Cheng knocked the man down with the flat of his blade. Two soldiers rushed to keep him from striking again; a third had already lifted the gate bar. He Cheng raised a foot to kick him, but someone shoved hard from behind, and he slammed against a pillar. The gate passage erupted in chaos. The leaves creaked against the crush of shoulders. By the time Lu Yan arrived, the gate had swung inward. He Cheng lay in the mud with a wound on his forehead. No one dared say whether it was a sword cut or a mark left by trampling feet.

People surged out while others ran after relatives; from outside the walls, parents carrying children rushed inward. Xu Sanniang fell repeatedly in the crowd, her boy too weak even to cry. Xu Cheng came limping down from the gate tower, his legs still sore from the beating, and finally drew his family aside against the wall. As they clung together, he saw men from his own unit fleeing as well.
“Back to camp!” government troops shouted in the distance.

Xu Cheng supported his wife with one hand and tightened the strap of his bow with the other. According to the military roll, he was still serving in camp. Leave today, and tomorrow he would be a deserter. Yet his child was gasping in his wife’s arms. How could he leave them beneath the gate?
Xu Sanniang saw his hesitation. She took the bow from his shoulder and placed it in his hands. “Keep it. Take us to the river first. Then decide whether you can come back.”

She did not urge her husband to rebel. Nor did she know whether the family could ever retrace its steps. Xu Cheng finally unstrung the bow, lifted the child onto his back, and followed the current of people toward the river.

Lu Yan rode out after them, repeatedly ordering his men to block the road. On the highway he saw relatives of his own officers among the refugees. Several soldiers obeyed by falling back to the roadside, but not one would shoot into the crowd. Anger made his throat ache. From the saddle he could only watch the Jin banner still flying above Xuyi as the ground below its walls slowly emptied.

When word reached the north bank, the Qin deputy again asked permission to lead cavalry across. Delay longer, he said, and someone would shut Xuyi’s gates once more. The commandant stood on the embankment for a long time before shaking his head. He ordered civilian boats requisitioned; physicians and granary clerks would board first. Shields could be carried, but bows must remain undrawn, and horses were not to enter the river.
“What if Jin soldiers fire arrows at refugees as they flee?”
“Get the people aboard first.”
“What if they shoot at our boats?”
The commandant paused. “Report it. Do not use the confusion as a pretext to attack the city.”

He too had imagined taking Xuyi without a battle. It would earn him a place in the record of military merit, perhaps glory enough for the rest of his life. But Chang’an’s written instruction was still tucked inside his belt. He could feel the stiff paper there as distinctly as he felt the registers for the soldiers and their grain behind him. If one man first broke an order expressly issued by the court, everyone afterward could claim a compelling reason to break it too.

When the first little boat from Qin came to the southern shore, Xu Sanniang stepped back with her child in her arms. A white-haired physician stood in the bow, shouting that the sick must board first. She asked whether crossing meant changing her family name, and whether her husband would be forced into the Qin army. The physician knew how to treat illness, not how to answer her. He summoned a granary clerk instead. Opening a wooden writing case, the clerk explained registration, temporary shelter, and separate examination for those who had served in an army. Even so, Xu Sanniang hesitated a moment longer.
“Can you give him medicine first?” she asked.
The physician reached for the child, wrapped him in cloth, and laid a hand on his burning forehead. “Get aboard first. A little longer, and it will be too late.”

Xu Cheng helped his wife into the boat and looked back from the gangplank. Atop Xuyi’s tower, the banner snapped in the evening wind. He slung his unstrung bow across his back and boarded last. As the boat pulled away, he saw old soldiers sitting stubbornly in the mud outside the east gate, as if staying where they were could mean the city had not been lost.

Opening the granaries had not ended Shanyang’s famine. The Qin grain would last a little more than twenty days. The date of the next boat shipment was entered in the accounts, but the salt and cloth needed for payment were still short. Du Qian spent his days pressing the villages for truthful figures and his nights worrying that another storm might delay the shipment and extinguish the gruel fires. At last a messenger came from Jiankang to investigate his dealings with Qin.

When Northern Garrison troops came to escort Du Qian away, the people crowded before the county granary. Some offered to bear his punishment; others offered salt and cloth from their homes to settle his debt. Du Qian told the registrar to continue the distributions, then handed over three account books, explaining each in turn: sick households in the red book, lodgers in the yellow, and salt and cloth assigned a cash value in the black. Whoever next took the county seal must first be shown those three books.

Liu Yu commanded the escort. The old sword at his waist had been worn pale with use. His few dozen men stood on the steps, leveling their long spears as the people pressed forward. Liu Yu ordered the points lowered and let the crowd stand along the street to say farewell.
“Magistrate Du,” Liu Yu said, “it is time to go.”
Du Qian looked at him. “Do you believe I deserve death, General?”
“The court ordered me to escort you. It did not order me to try your case.”

He refused to put Du Qian in a wooden cangue, had his hands tied in front, and allowed him provisions for the road. His deputy grumbled that such leniency would be difficult to explain at headquarters. Liu Yu said he would report it himself. The people opened a narrow passage, women with children lining either side. At the end of the street, Du Qian heard the wooden grain measure strike once more at the granary. He turned: the clerks had begun weighing grain again.

On the third night, the escort halted at an abandoned relay station. Half its roof tiles were gone, stagnant water covered the ground, and the single well in the courtyard was nearly dry. The soldiers boiled two sacks of mixed grain and shared the food. Leaning against the wall with his bowl of gruel, Du Qian asked why Jingkou’s soldiers were also owed provisions. Liu Yu told him it was not a question for a prisoner to ask on the road. Du Qian smiled and asked another: if the court made opening a granary a crime, who would dare save the next person from starvation?
“Some men open granaries to buy loyalty,” Liu Yu replied.
“True,” Du Qian said. “That is why you must examine my three ledgers.”
Liu Yu studied him. Du Qian said no more and drank the last mouthful of thin gruel. Suddenly dogs barked outside. An arrow came through a broken window and buried itself in the lamp post.

Dozens of starving refugees and army deserters burst into the courtyard, shouting that grain was hidden inside. Others shouted that Magistrate Du must be freed. The Northern Garrison men hastily formed ranks. A blade flashed over the wet ground; a bloodied wooden spear fell at their feet. Liu Yu stood in front, wrenched a sword from one assailant, and ordered his soldiers to hold the courtyard without pursuing and slaughtering those who scattered into the woods.

Among the captives was a youth who said he had served in Xuyi’s Left Camp and that his mother had crossed the river. His uniform hung in rags across his back, and his fists were clenched as though opening them would invite someone to hack off his fingers. The deputy wanted him beheaded as an example. Liu Yu ordered him tied to a pillar and his wounds bandaged first. Seven attackers lay dead in the courtyard, and five of Liu Yu’s men were wounded. Once the fighting was over, Du Qian sat inside with the rope at his wrists rubbed deep into raw flesh.
“Why were those people looking for you?” Liu Yu asked.
“Because the crossing at Shanyang was not closed.”
“And after they take you away?”
“I do not know.”
Liu Yu stood in the room for a moment, then drew his sword and severed the knot. Du Qian looked up as though seeing this officer clearly for the first time.

“Take the old riverbed behind the station,” Liu Yu said quietly. “Follow the withered willows to the north embankment, then turn east to reach Shanyang. If the authorities capture you again, I cannot save you.”
Du Qian remained seated. “If you let me return, how will you answer for it in Jingkou?”
“Deserters attacked the station last night. The prisoner went missing.”
“Military law will question you.”
“It will.”
At last Du Qian rose. He stopped again at the doorway, turned, and asked, “General, why would you risk punishment on my account?”

Liu Yu did not think the answer that came to him sounded like a general’s. He could see only the two lines of people waiting for grain outside the Shanyang granary, and Du Qian, even as he was taken away, making sure those three ledgers would be kept.
“If you have not stolen the grain for yourself,” he said, “the people of Shanyang still need you.”

Du Qian said no more. A thin new moon hung above the ruined wall, and wild mugwort reached his knees as he walked north alone. The next morning the deputy discovered that the prisoner had escaped and demanded that riders be sent after him at once. Liu Yu ordered the dead buried and the wounded tended first. Then he entered the attack and Du Qian’s escape in his military report. He did not execute the young deserter and present him as the culprit.

Once he sent the report, he knew this would not end quietly. The military office at Jingkou would demand answers, and so would Jiankang. If Shanyang kept its granaries open, Du Qian would sooner or later face government soldiers again. Many footprints led north through the river mud; where several trod the same place, the impressions held small pools of water. Liu Yu examined the edge of his sword, nicked in the night fighting, and ordered the column to continue south.
